misconceptions.name: Variable Assignment Confusion
misconceptions.description: Student misunderstands the unidirectional flow of assignment (`variable = expression`), treating it as algebraic equality or attempting to write `expression = variable` (e.g., `x + 1 = x` or swapping source and target).
observable_symptoms: Inverting left and right sides of assignment statements
Believing `a = b` simultaneously changes both variables or makes them permanently coupled
Writing equations like `a + 5 = b` instead of `b = a + 5`
common_errors: SyntaxError: cannot assign to operator or literal
Overwriting target value before reading it (e.g. naive swap: `a = b; b = a`)
Expecting earlier variable to automatically recompute when dependent variables change
diagnostic_patterns: Left-hand side of assignment AST is not a Name or Attribute
Learner explanation uses symmetric phrasing ('a equals b', 'sets both to be equal')
Naive variable swap without temp variable or simultaneous tuple unpacking

intervention_strategy.action: Trace memory boxes showing explicit value copy from right-hand expression into left-hand variable slot.
Show sequential updates where updating `b` does not alter `a` after `a = b`.

resolution_criteria: Correctly executes two-variable swaps with temporary variables or tuple unpacking
Accurately predicts output of sequential reassignments without permanent coupling assumptions
Writes correct assignment syntax with single target identifier on left-hand side

misconceptions.name: Variable Scope Confusion
misconceptions.description: Student confuses local function scope with global scope, expecting variables defined inside a function to be accessible outside, or conversely expecting function-level assignments to automatically mutate outer variables without returning them.
observable_symptoms: Attempting to read local function variables from the global scope after function call
Modifying a parameter inside a function and expecting caller's variable to change without re-assignment or return
Unintentionally shadowing global variables with local variables of the same name
common_errors: NameError: name 'x' is not defined (when accessing local variable outside)
UnboundLocalError: local variable referenced before assignment
Function returns None while student assumes outer variables were mutated
diagnostic_patterns: AST accesses identifier defined strictly inside FunctionDef scope from Module body
Learner claims outer variable 'now has the value from the function' without re-binding return value
Omits return statement assuming function acts as an in-place macro

intervention_strategy.action: Visualize call stack frames: showing frame creation on function entry and frame destruction upon return.
Demonstrate that assigning `x = 100` inside a function leaves global `x` untouched.

resolution_criteria: Correctly distinguishes variables inside stack frames from module-level scope
Appropriately captures return values to update caller state
Solves variable shadowing puzzles with 100% trace accuracy

misconceptions.name: Loop Boundary / Off-by-One
misconceptions.description: Student misunderstands loop stopping boundaries (especially zero-indexing and exclusive upper bounds such as in `range(n)` or `<= len(list)`), executing the loop body one time too many or one time too few.
observable_symptoms: Iterating up to `<= len(arr)` leading to out-of-bounds error on final index
Expecting `range(1, 5)` to include 5 (producing 5 iterations instead of 4)
Missing the first element (index 0) by initializing iteration variable to 1
common_errors: IndexError: list index out of range
Summation / accumulator is missing first or last item
Loop runs n-1 or n+1 times instead of expected n
diagnostic_patterns: AST BinaryOp condition `< index <= len(items)` or `range(0, len(items) + 1)`
Learner explanation claims 'range(a, b) includes both a and b'
Execution trace fails on final index boundary

intervention_strategy.action: Compare `list(range(5))` which yields `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]` (5 items total) against student expected values.
Step through loop index by index, annotating the exact termination condition check on the final iteration.

resolution_criteria: Correctly predicts exact number of iterations and values generated by arbitrary `range(start, stop, step)`
Safely bounds array index loops without IndexError
Distinguishes inclusive mathematical intervals from half-open programming intervals

misconceptions.name: Loop Condition Misunderstanding
misconceptions.description: Student misunderstands when a loop condition is evaluated, believing that a loop terminates immediately the instant a condition becomes false in the middle of the loop body, or confusing while-loop 'continuation condition' with an 'exit condition'.
observable_symptoms: Believing a loop aborts mid-body rather than finishing the current iteration
Inverting while-loop condition (writing the stopping condition instead of continuation condition)
Writing infinite loops because the termination condition can never become false at the header evaluation point
common_errors: Infinite loop (TimeoutError)
Premature loop exit assumption
Statements after condition violation within body executed unexpectedly
diagnostic_patterns: While test expression negated from desired continuation logic
Learner reasoning states: 'It stopped at line 3 as soon as x became 5'
Execution timeout caused by loop variable not progressing towards condition false

intervention_strategy.action: Illustrate execution step-by-step showing that statements below the updated variable in the body still execute until the loop header is reached again.
Prompt learner: 'Is while (x < 5) a condition to KEEP GOING or a condition to STOP?'

resolution_criteria: Correctly describes the discrete evaluation points of loop headers
Correctly formulates continuation predicates for complex while loops
Accurately traces all statements executed on the final body pass

misconceptions.name: Conditional Logic Misunderstanding
misconceptions.description: Student misinterprets conditional branching flow, such as assuming multiple independent `if` statements behave like `if/elif/else`, or misunderstanding the mutually exclusive nature of `if/elif/else` ladders.
observable_symptoms: Using sequential `if` statements when mutually exclusive branches are intended, causing multiple blocks to fire
Assuming `else` attaches to the first `if` instead of the nearest preceding unclosed conditional block
Believing all branches are evaluated simultaneously
common_errors: State overwritten by subsequent `if` block matching newly modified state
Unreachable code in conditional branches
Incorrect branch execution in chained comparisons
diagnostic_patterns: Multiple top-level If nodes without Elif/Orelse modifying the same target state
Learner reasoning asserts 'Only one if can run in a program'
Execution hits multiple blocks when only one action was desired

intervention_strategy.action: Trace control flow through separate `if` statements versus an `if-elif-else` chain, highlighting branch skipping.
Provide code where first `if` modifies a variable such that the second `if` immediately evaluates to True.

resolution_criteria: Correctly explains why subsequent `if` blocks execute even if an earlier `if` succeeded
Selects `elif` appropriately for mutually exclusive alternatives
Correctly traces order of evaluation through branching ladders

misconceptions.name: Boolean Operator Misunderstanding
misconceptions.description: Student misunderstands Boolean precedence or operator semantics, especially writing natural language phrasing like `if x == 1 or 2` (evaluating truthiness of `2` rather than `x == 2`), or confusing `and` vs `or` logic and short-circuit evaluation.
observable_symptoms: Writing `if x == 'a' or 'b'` expecting both comparisons to check equality to `x`
Confusing `and` with `or` in compound boundary checks (e.g. `x < 0 and x > 10`)
Misunderstanding operator precedence between `not`, `and`, and `or`
common_errors: Condition always evaluates to True because non-empty string or non-zero integer is truthy
Condition never evaluates to True due to mutually impossible `and` expressions
Short-circuit evaluation skipped or misunderstood
diagnostic_patterns: AST contains `BoolOp(Or, [Compare(x, Eq, a), Constant(b)])`
Learner claims `if x == 1 or 2:` checks if x is either 1 or 2
Condition evaluates to True regardless of `x` value

intervention_strategy.action: Evaluate `bool('b')` or `bool(2)` independently in Python to show why `x == 1 or 2` always evaluates as True.
Guide learner to formulate full Boolean comparison: `x == 1 or x == 2` or `x in (1, 2)`.

resolution_criteria: Correctly identifies why `x == a or b` is flawed
Correctly translates compound domain restrictions into syntactically sound Boolean conjunctions and disjunctions
Accurately evaluates truth values under short-circuit evaluation rules

misconceptions.name: Return vs Print Confusion
misconceptions.description: Student conflates printing to standard output with returning a value from a function, believing `print()` passes data back to the caller or that `return` displays text on the terminal screen.
observable_symptoms: Writing functions that `print(result)` without `return`, then attempting to store the call in a variable (getting `None`)
Expecting `return x` to automatically print `x` on standard console output in a standalone script
Placing code after a `return` statement expecting it to execute
common_errors: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for NoneType and int
Output contains extra 'None' when doing `print(my_func())`
Unreachable code warnings after early return
diagnostic_patterns: FunctionDef body terminates with Call to print instead of Return
Caller assigns result of void function: `res = func()` followed by `res + 1`
Learner explanation says 'The function returned the printed number to the screen'

intervention_strategy.action: Show that `val = print(5)` sets `val = None`, while `val = return_five()` sets `val = 5`.
Contrast console output display (ephemeral user interface) with programmatic data return (passing data between code components).

resolution_criteria: Consistently uses `return` for values intended for downstream computation
Correctly predicts that calling a function containing only `print` evaluates to `None` in expressions
Understands that `return` immediately terminates function execution

misconceptions.name: Parameter vs Argument Confusion
misconceptions.description: Student confuses formal parameters (function definition placeholders) with actual arguments (values passed at call time), believing parameter names must match argument variable names, or using undefined variables as parameters.
observable_symptoms: Believing caller variable must be renamed to match function definition parameter name
Passing undefined identifiers as arguments instead of literals or bound variables
Hardcoding values inside function body instead of utilizing the passed parameter variables
common_errors: NameError: name 'parameter_name' is not defined at call site
Ignoring passed arguments by reading fixed global variables
Refusing to reuse a generic function because argument variable names differ
diagnostic_patterns: Function defines parameter `x`, but body uses global variable `a` directly
Learner asserts: 'I had to name my variable x because the function parameter is x'
Call site passes string `'x'` when variable `x` was intended

intervention_strategy.action: Compare a function to a recipe: the recipe ingredient placeholder ('flour') works whether you bring brand A or brand B.
Trace function call mapping: caller variable `age = 25` bound to parameter `num` inside the function activation record.

resolution_criteria: Correctly invokes functions with varying argument names and expressions
Writes general-purpose functions relying exclusively on parameter names rather than external global names
Accurately maps positional and keyword arguments to parameters

misconceptions.name: List/Array Indexing Misunderstanding
misconceptions.description: Student misunderstands zero-based list indexing or slice semantics, confusing an element's 1-based ordinal position with its index, or confusing list elements with their index positions.
observable_symptoms: Accessing `items[1]` expecting the first element instead of `items[0]`
Treating element value as the index (e.g. `items[item]` where item is a string/object)
Misunderstanding slice endpoint `items[0:3]` expecting 4 elements
common_errors: TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str
IndexError: list index out of range on `items[len(items)]`
Off-by-one element retrieval in sequential access
diagnostic_patterns: AST Subscript using element iterator instead of index integer
`arr[len(arr)]` lookup in code
Learner states 'items[1] is the first item in the list'

intervention_strategy.action: Display memory index grid: Index 0 -> First Item, Index 1 -> Second Item, showing `len(arr) - 1` as final item.
Differentiate `for item in items:` (accesses values) from `for i in range(len(items)):` (generates indices).

resolution_criteria: Correctly retrieves first, last, and nth elements without index errors
Distinguishes element values from their integer positional indices
Accurately computes sub-slice lengths using `stop - start`

misconceptions.name: Mutable State / Reference Confusion
misconceptions.description: Student misunderstands reference semantics and mutable objects, believing list assignment creates an independent copy (`b = a`) or that modifying a list in a function won't affect the caller's object.
observable_symptoms: Performing `b = a` and being surprised when `b.append(x)` also modifies `a`
Believing `list(a)` or `a[:]` is identical to reference alias `b = a`
Creating lists of lists with repeated references (e.g. `[[0]*3]*3`) and wondering why changing one row alters all rows
common_errors: Unexpected data corruption across aliased references
Failed deep copy vs shallow copy behavior
Unintentional side-effects in function arguments
diagnostic_patterns: Assignment `list2 = list1` followed by in-place mutation (`.append()`, `.sort()`, `[i] = ...`)
Multiplied list references `[[]] * n`
Learner explanation: 'b is a separate copy of a'

intervention_strategy.action: Draw heap reference arrows: both variables `a` and `b` pointing to the exact same list object ID in memory.
Print `id(a) == id(b)` for reference alias versus `id(a) == id(a.copy())` for shallow copy.

resolution_criteria: Correctly predicts state changes across aliased reference variables
Applies `.copy()`, slicing `[:]`, or `copy.deepcopy()` appropriately when mutation isolation is needed
Understands in-place mutation methods vs methods returning new objects
